title: What `Predicate` does `filter()` accept, and how does `filter()` work internally (lazy, spliterator, predicate test)?
shortTitle: filter() — what Predicate it accepts, how it works internally (lazy, spliterator, predicate test)

s1_definition.profdef: `Stream.filter(Predicate<? super T> predicate)` accepts a `Predicate<T>` — a functional interface with one method `boolean test(T t)`. It returns a new `Stream<T>` containing ONLY elements where `predicate.test(element)` returns true. Internally: filter is LAZY — calling it just wraps the upstream source in a new `StatelessOp` pipeline stage. When a terminal triggers, the stream's `Spliterator` pulls elements one-at-a-time from the source. For each element, `predicate.test(element)` is called — if true, the element is pushed downstream to the next stage; if false, it is DROPPED and the spliterator pulls the next element. No intermediate collection is created. The Spliterator is the underlying engine that drives element traversal: `tryAdvance(Consumer)` pulls one element, `forEachRemaining(Consumer)` pulls all, and `trySplit()` divides the source for parallel processing.
s1_definition.analogy: `filter()` is the bank's KYC verification clerk sitting on the conveyor belt. Each customer application arrives one-at-a-time (spliterator pulls). The clerk checks "does this customer pass KYC?" (predicate.test). If YES → pass to the next station. If NO → reject and pull the next application. The clerk does NOT start checking until the manager (terminal operation) says "begin processing." The clerk never collects all applications first — each one is checked and passed/rejected immediately.
s1_definition.oneliner: filter(Predicate) = keep elements where test() returns true. Lazy StatelessOp. Spliterator pulls one-at-a-time. No intermediate collection. Predicate supports and/or/negate composition.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's transaction monitoring system applies layered filters to detect suspicious activity.** Layer 1: completed transactions only. Layer 2: amount above Rs.50,000. Layer 3: international transfers. Layer 4: new accounts (< 30 days old). The old code had nested if-statements 4 levels deep. The team uses composed Predicates with filter() — each layer is a named Predicate combined with `.and()`, making the rules readable, testable, and independently reusable.

**What the project will show:** filter() with simple lambda, method reference, composed Predicate (and/or/negate), Predicate<? super T> wildcard, custom Spliterator demonstration, and the lazy stateless nature with execution tracking.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** 7 transactions loaded. Stream created — lazy pipeline with 3 filter stages.

**Step 2 — Terminal .toList() triggers.** Spliterator pulls TXN-001 from source.

**Step 3 — Layer 1 (isCompleted).** TXN-001 status=COMPLETED → true → passes to Layer 2.

**Step 4 — Layer 2 (amount>50K OR highRisk).** TXN-001 Rs.500, India → false AND false → dropped. Spliterator pulls TXN-002.

**Step 5.** TXN-002: L1 completed (Recommended) . L2 Rs.75,000 > 50K (Recommended) . L3 accountAge=400 > 30 → dropped. Not a new account.

**Step 6.** TXN-003: L1 completed (Recommended) . L2 Rs.15L > 50K (Recommended) AND Nigeria is high-risk (Recommended) . L3 accountAge=15 < 30 → PASS (Caution) . This is the ONE suspicious transaction.

**Step 7.** TXN-007: L1 status=FAILED → dropped immediately. Layers 2 and 3 NEVER run for this transaction. This is the stateless, fused behavior.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ filter() INTERNAL MECHANICS ═══

  trades.stream().filter(Trade::isSettled)
    │
    ├─ Creates: ReferencePipeline$StatelessOp
    │           wraps upstream source
    │           stores predicate reference
    │           does NOT execute yet!
    │
    └─ When terminal triggers:
         Spliterator.tryAdvance(element) → pulls ONE element from source
           │
           predicate.test(element)
           ├─ true  → downstream.accept(element) → passes to next stage
           └─ false → DROPPED (element simply not passed forward)
           │
           Spliterator.tryAdvance() → pulls NEXT element
           ... repeat until source exhausted or short-circuit

  ═══ LAYERED vs COMPOSED FILTER ═══

  LAYERED (3 separate filter calls — same result, but 3 pipeline stages):
    .filter(isCompleted)
    .filter(amountAbove(50K).or(isHighRisk))
    .filter(isNewAccount(30))

  COMPOSED (1 filter call — single pipeline stage):
    .filter(isCompleted.and(amountAbove(50K).or(isHighRisk)).and(isNewAccount(30)))

  Performance: nearly identical — both are fused into single pass.
  Readability: layered is clearer when logging each layer separately.
  Testability: composed Predicate can be unit-tested independently.

  ═══ PREDICATE COMPOSITION ═══

  Predicate<T>
    .and(other)   → this.test(t) && other.test(t)    (short-circuit: if this=false, skip other)
    .or(other)    → this.test(t) || other.test(t)    (short-circuit: if this=true, skip other)
    .negate()     → !this.test(t)
    Predicate.not(pred) → !pred.test(t)              (Java 11 static method)

  ═══ SPLITERATOR — THE ENGINE ═══

  Spliterator<T>
    .tryAdvance(Consumer)     → pull ONE element, return true/false
    .forEachRemaining(Consumer) → pull ALL remaining
    .trySplit()                → split for parallel (ForkJoinPool)
    .estimateSize()            → approximate remaining count
    .characteristics()         → ORDERED, SIZED, DISTINCT, SORTED, etc.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The filter method accepts a `Predicate<? super T>`, which means it can take a Predicate of the stream's element type or any supertype. It returns a new Stream containing only elements where predicate.test returns true. Internally, filter is a stateless lazy operation — calling it just creates a new StatelessOp pipeline stage that stores the predicate reference. No element is tested until a terminal operation triggers the pipeline. When triggered, the underlying Spliterator pulls elements one at a time: tryAdvance pulls one element, the predicate tests it, and if true it passes downstream; if false it is silently dropped.

In my transaction monitoring service, I demonstrate both layered filtering (three separate filter calls, each with logging) and composed filtering (one filter call with a composed Predicate built from and/or/negate). Both produce identical results because stream fusion processes each element through all stages in a single pass regardless. The layered approach is better for debugging because you can log each layer's pass/drop independently. The composed approach is better for unit testing because the Predicate can be tested in isolation without a stream.

The Spliterator is the low-level engine that drives all stream traversal. For sequential streams, tryAdvance pulls one element at a time. For parallel streams, trySplit divides the source into two halves that can be processed by separate ForkJoinPool threads. The Predicate interface supports composition with and, or, and negate — these create new Predicate instances that combine the original predicates with short-circuit boolean logic: and stops on first false, or stops on first true. Named Predicates stored as static factory methods in a FilterRules class are reusable across different streams and independently testable.
